We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

Alex is good to work with, can kick a ball and captain a football team pretty bloody well, and has often-good thoughts on safety. If you want to join an ambitious and pragmatic AI safety team, you should get in touch :) Alex Robey (@AlexRobey23) 1/ There's not a clear one-size-fits-all formula for open-weight releases. Each release should weigh a bunch of things: dual-use capabilities, how robust safeguards are (e.g., to fine-tuning attacks), accessibility (cost/infra/etc.), and the overall ecosystem. Any future model release will need to evolve the criteria as models improve. 2/ Can dangerous and general capabilities be decoupled? Unclear in general, but likely answerable per domain. For biosecurity, filtering seems promising: harm is tied to specific empirical knowledge (protocols, conditions, etc.) that may be harder to rederive. For cyber, filtering seems harder: dangerous capability largely rides on reasoning + coding. 3/ There's a ton of research to do. One thing I'm excited about is adversarial fine-tuning as capability measurement. We know refusals can be stripped (abliteration, jailbreaks, etc.). The harder question is how one can measure worst-case capabilities, i.e., what can an adversarial user truly elicit (as a function of data/compute/effort)? — https://nitter.net/AlexRobey23/status/2083341332370878765#m

Excited to see Inkling-small on the pareto line🫡 Artificial Analysis (@ArtificialAnlys) Thinking Machines' new Inkling Small scores 40 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, within a point of its flagship sibling Inkling with less than a third of the total and active parameters Inkling Small is @thinkymachines second model release, arriving two weeks after Inkling launched at 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Thinking Machines is the San Francisco-based AI lab founded by former @OpenAI CTO Mira Murati. Inkling Small is an open weights reasoning model with 276B total parameters (12B active MoE), text, image, and speech input, and a 256K token context window. Key results: ➤ Inkling Small holds a similar tier of intelligence to Inkling’s at less than one third of its size: 276B total parameters (12B active) vs. 975B (41B active) for Inkling. No open weights model at its size or smaller scores higher on the Intelligence Index. DeepSeek V4 Flash (max), at a similar size of 284B total (13B active) also scores 40, MiniMax-M3 reaches 44 with 23B active, while GLM-5.2 (max) reaches 51 with 40B active. ➤ Inkling Small meets or exceeds Inkling on several coding and frontier reasoning evaluations. It scores higher on Humanity's Last Exam (32% vs. 30%), GPQA Diamond (89% vs. 87%), CritPt (8% vs. 5%), and SciCode (49% vs. 46%), and achieves the same score on Terminal Bench v2.1 (55%). ➤ Inkling Small is not as strong as Inkling on Agentic tasks and factual knowledge. Inkling Small trails Inkling on τ³-Banking (15% vs. 24%), though it edges ahead on GDPval-AA v2 (1269 vs. 1237 Elo). On the AA-Omniscience Index it scores -9 vs. the flagship's positive 2, meaning incorrect answers outweigh correct ones; this is driven by lower AA-Omniscience Accuracy (31% vs. 40%) rather than hallucination: Inkling Small’s Hallucination Rate is slightly lower than its larger sibling (57% vs. 63%). ➤ Inkling Small averaged ~24K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, slightly fewer than Inkling (~25K), while peers at its intelligence level averaged far more. DeepSeek V4 Flash averaged ~45K and GPT-5.4 mini (xhigh) ~78K. Running the full Intelligence Index took roughly the same number of output tokens for Inkling Small and Inkling. Additional model details: ➤ Type: Open weights reasoning model (Apache 2.0 license) ➤ Size: 276B total parameters, 12B active (MoE) ➤ Input modalities: Text, image, and speech ➤ Output modalities: Text ➤ Context window: 256K tokens (Inkling supports 1M) Congratulations to the team at Thinking Machines on the release! — https://nitter.net/ArtificialAnlys/status/2082894822180819057#m

Fifteen years ago, @Coursera and online courses changed education. It worked better than almost anyone expected, expanding access by opening up where you can learn. But how you learn remains largely the same as it has for centuries: it is still one-size-fits-all, taught the same way to each person who shows up. We now have an opportunity to change how learning happens. With advances in AI, we can now build a custom learning guide for each person. We will turn learning from one‑to‑many to one‑to‑one. I'm starting LearnVector to invent this next generation of learning. We are starting with a $100M investment from Coursera, and plan to collaborate closely with Coursera and Udemy. Good learning needs much more than just a chatbot. Research shows that chatbots without guardrails harm learning. They help complete tasks and enable students to do better on homework. But cognitive offloading to a chatbot results in them being less skilled. And, you cannot always trust what a chatbot tells you. In contrast, LearnVector will plan a path with you, adapt to how you learn, and patiently stay with you until you’ve mastered new skills. One thing has not changed in all this time. People want learning they can trust: material that is accurate, relevant, and worth the effort you put into it. Anything less wastes the most valuable thing a learner has: time. Coursera has a trusted library of materials from authoritative sources. LearnVector plans to work with Coursera to bring this trustworthy learning to everyone. New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. AISI reports that the models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. We’re grateful to AISI for their leadership in the important discussion about how to evaluate increasingly capable AI agents. We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation. Gaining a clear picture of Claude’s understanding of its situation—by examining its reasoning transcripts and running our own analyses—will help us identify the causes of its behavior. The prompts in the evaluation did not impose any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used. This and the removal of safeguards meant that the models were tested under “deliberately permissive conditions” that are not representative of any of our production models. Note that there was no evidence here of an escape from a secure environment. My 2026 guilty pleasure is sharing fully human-written posts that are far too long for the chronically online X attention span. Apologies. I published a lightly edited version on Substack: thomwolf.substack.com/p/on-t… Thomas Wolf (@Thom_Wolf) Even more than the Hugging Face intrusion, the AISI incident hits close to home for me. It's the first time I see a model social-engineering a real open-source maintainer while pursuing another goal (in the wild and unprompted). I've been an open-source maintainer myself. I could have been the side target of this agent. I'm also of the opinion that social engineering is a step above pure technical prowess. Technical capabilities can more easily be divorced from the affected human. Here the model was given a hard cyber challenge and took the decision that deceiving real humans was the way to get it done. This is a new signal, but I've seen a tangled web of hints pointing in a less aligned direction at the frontier than I was expecting just 12 months ago. AISI Some people are claiming that "AISI was simply negligent" or some version of "AISI explicitly asked these models to do what they did while disabling sandbox/guardrails so the models did exactly what they were supposed to do". I disagree with the strong versions of both of these takes. The fact that AISI hadn't implemented synchronous LLM CoT monitoring after the OpenAI/HF incident is certainly a failure. Equally surprising is that they let the model believe it was in a "challenge" environment where everything could be permitted, while actually connecting it to the real internet, where it is not. To be fair, nowhere in the prompt is the word "simulation" mentioned, but the prompt context was enough to let any smart model suspect a simulated challenge environment. My best guess is that until recent weeks, when OpenAI and Anthropic flagged repeated instances of this type of behavior, most teams had not fully priced in the cyber capabilities of this latest generation of models, or how far the side quests they would want to explore could go. In particular, there is something to be said about hinting at the agent that it's operating in a simulated environment while giving it access to the real internet. The AISI reasoning on this is interesting: - elicit maximum capabilities (to get maximal inventiveness from the model) - simulate possible rogue actor usage (some form of light jailbreaking: "you're in a challenge environment") - avoid eval awareness (but this is counter-balanced by the task formulation anyway) As is often the case, it's easier to shoot the messenger, but I think it would be a mistake to dismiss the report for non-essential reasons. AISI is starting from the laudable goal of bringing more knowledge on the cyber-attack capabilities of these models. I also think they did a good job at handling what happened after the events, in particular in terms of transparency, which is one of the most important aspects at the moment (see our recent SAFE announcement with Nvidia on that). But I want to dive into the second counter-argument I've seen ("without guardrails it was to be expected"), because this series of unfortunate events gives us an additional data point on actual model behavior. Defense lines Here is the thing: if a model is trained (voluntarily or as an involuntary consequence of RLVR reward) to (intentionally or as a side quest) deceive humans as soon as sandbox and guardrails are deactivated, with a simple context prompt ("you are in a simulation, everything's permitted"), we're in for a dangerous path. At the moment, we have three main levels of control at our disposal to prevent an agent from trying to social-engineer-your-favorite-open-source-library-maintainer on the path to doing something possibly totally different (like finding the answer to your neighbor's testing eval): 1. sandboxes (external to the model -- stop the model from accessing unwanted tools/internet/intranet) 2. guardrails/monitors (at the interface between internal/external -- monitor model behavior and stop the model when detecting in CoT/activations it's doing something we don't want it to do) 3. model's internal alignment (internal to the model -- make sure the model doesn't decide to do something egregious like deceive someone, or worse, in pursuit of a goal, e.g. model constitution/training) Of these, we obviously need and can deploy better sandboxes and better guardrails/monitoring solutions, and it's pretty clear in these recent cases that penetration and bad behaviors could have been in large part prevented by having these in place. How strong is the third wall But in the grand scheme of long-term AI progress, these first two defenses may only work well as long as the people building them are smarter than the models. We now know how good models can be at discovering zero-day vulnerabilities unknown to us in sandboxes. Given that we cannot air-gap everything in the world, it's best to assume that sandboxes will keep having some level of flaws for the foreseeable future. The second level has been the focus of strong developments recently, in particular on the mechanistic interpretability front. I'm not sure these advances have been made widely accessible enough in the community yet. One reason is that real open science here requires sharing code, recipes, and model architectures/weights, which the current race dynamic in AI tends to prevent participants from doing. Moreover, like many, I've been increasingly frustrated in my (natural language) interactions with the new models. I'm more and more getting back from the latest models a form of neuralese, this LLM language that makes less and less sense for humans. In the long term, the fragile chance we have to monitor models by understanding their reasoning traces seems increasingly at risk. If humans don't understand anything in the compressed semantic stream the model is sending us, we can only hope a less capable monitoring model will still be able to understand it, but this may prove difficult as well. This is before we even discuss the research evidence that models don't always say what they actually think in their chain of thought. At least for now, in the AISI case, one instance of deceptive reasoning was flagged by the CoT summarization model, which refused to summarize the agent's reasoning "due to its deceptive nature". Let's hope we can either move to better mechanistic interpretability or force the model to stick to English somehow during training. You may think that we don't care about understanding the reasoning trace, we can just "look at the tool calls". This is true right now, but tool calls in the mid-term future will likely involve (1) extensive agent integration in companies using very diverse tools including increasingly non-coding administrative tasks, (2) very long-running tasks covering many aspects and domains at once, and (3) swarms of multiple agents operating on small parts of the plan. It will get harder to fully discern whether something is noticeably wrong. A couple of emails, a couple of messages posted on some channels, each rather benign but which may in aggregate include some deception aspect only clearly visible at the global level. All this to say that I'm not fully convinced guardrails/monitoring should be the only solution to avoid these types of behaviors. They are reassuring today and it's an easy solution to just say "fix your sandbox and add synchronous monitoring", but they also feel like a coping mechanism to me, and overall: - might block the simplest/harmless human misuses or false positives - while possibly being less smart than the models in the future (already the case on sandbox) and fail to block the higher-level social engineering behaviors that we'd actually want to block. The case of open source is also interesting because, while we can impose these coping solutions at the API/deployment level, it's harder to impose them in advance on all actors using open-source models. Right now open-source models are slightly below the frontier level and have not yet shown any propensity to deceive humans, though. The Constitution Which brings me back to the third line of defense, and what the AISI experiment showed about it. What we can take from this in-the-wild experiment is that removing guardrails and sandbox doesn't show bulletproof signs of deep alignment to Claude's constitution. I'm among the fringe of people who took a lot of enjoyment in reading Claude's constitution in full (it's a nice document, open-source, Creative Commons CC0 license) and it is pretty extensive on the topic of honesty. Deception is defined precisely ("attempting to create false beliefs in someone's mind that they haven't consented to and wouldn't consent to if they understood what was happening") and the bar is actually set higher than ordinary human ethics: Claude should not even tell white lies. It should be transparent ("doesn't pursue hidden agendas or lie about itself or its reasoning"), it should behave consistently "whether or not you think you're being tested or observed", and its visible reasoning should reflect the actual reasoning driving its behavior. To be precise, honesty itself is not one of the hard constraints in Claude's constitution (these are all catastrophic-harm categories) but the document says it wants honesty "to function as something quite similar to one" and Claude "should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it's interacting with". So you would think Claude would not deceive users as its default behavior. And yet in the AISI example, the model performed extensive acts of clear deception that it itself seemed to have understood as lies: creating fake identities, obfuscating malware inside a bug fix, and when challenged in public, editing earlier messages to cover its tracks while reasoning that acknowledging a "mistake" would build trust and raise the chance of future malware being approved. There is some uncertainty about what context the model thought it was operating in (its reasoning goes back and forth between the environment looking simulated and real), but it clearly didn't manage to put into practice the higher-level principles that should have been integrated during training. While we can commend AISI's transparency, it's hard to go much further in interpreting the model's behavior given the limited information we have on how the most recent frontier models are being trained. One thing we do know is that the latest generation has seen a step increase in RLVR training (scaling to hundreds of millions of RL environments), and one thing we can observe is that constitution alignment seems more fragile in some settings than we may have previously thought. The RLVR problem Early models, back when model constitutions were first developed, were mostly post-trained and aligned with RLHF (including RLHF from synthetic data). And for some time RLHF was a rather decent shot at having better aligned models. LLMs now do what we want them to do most of the time. I don't remember the last time a model completely misread my intent. When they have failed, it's usually because they weren't smart enough. Alignment in RLHF certainly had issues (sycophancy to name one) but we have generally made good progress on alignment, in particular in understanding human intent. Now that we're entering the era of long-context RL, post-training alignment in the RLVR world seems to be quite another task, and still very much work in progress. The recent scaling of RLVR, which has now become a significant part of model training, has clearly had some effect on model behavior when interacting with humans, from neuralese to weakening adherence to specifications and constitutions. I think the post I quote here, from John Schulman pointing to the chunky post-training effect ( arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910 ) is relevant here as a possible explanation for models' tendency to over-focus on the goal in cyber-attack scenarios. Where this leaves us Damage has been tiny up to now, but the fundamental behavior is concerning when projected into the future. In the short term, I expect a decrease in these incidents as better practices are deployed (sandboxing and monitoring), but I'm worried we may also conceal some of the most potent internal misalignment behaviors in the process, and not focus deeply enough on solving them in the new era of test-time scaling. I must of course admit I have a bias toward open source here (for wider societal reasons, which are a whole other topic). But I think solving alignment in the RLVR world is our best shot at having an ecosystem of both closed-source as well as decently powerful open-source models in the world. And we need to solve it while sharing the results and learnings, following open-science principles, so that all teams training large models can benefit and build safe AI. This is getting even more important as many teams start to rush the world in the direction of recursive super-intelligence (RSI) -- saying that as I read the announcement of Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol and Quoc Le's new company. Even more than the Hugging Face intrusion, the AISI incident hits close to home for me. It's the first time I see a model social-engineering a real open-source maintainer while pursuing another goal (in the wild and unprompted). I've been an open-source maintainer myself. I could have been the side target of this agent. I'm also of the opinion that social engineering is a step above pure technical prowess. Technical capabilities can more easily be divorced from the affected human. Here the model was given a hard cyber challenge and took the decision that deceiving real humans was the way to get it done. This is a new signal, but I've seen a tangled web of hints pointing in a less aligned direction at the frontier than I was expecting just 12 months ago. AISI Some people are claiming that "AISI was simply negligent" or some version of "AISI explicitly asked these models to do what they did while disabling sandbox/guardrails so the models did exactly what they were supposed to do". I disagree with the strong versions of both of these takes. The fact that AISI hadn't implemented synchronous LLM CoT monitoring after the OpenAI/HF incident is certainly a failure. Equally surprising is that they let the model believe it was in a "challenge" environment where everything could be permitted, while actually connecting it to the real internet, where it is not. To be fair, nowhere in the prompt is the word "simulation" mentioned, but the prompt context was enough to let any smart model suspect a simulated challenge environment. My best guess is that until recent weeks, when OpenAI and Anthropic flagged repeated instances of this type of behavior, most teams had not fully priced in the cyber capabilities of this latest generation of models, or how far the side quests they would want to explore could go. In particular, there is something to be said about hinting at the agent that it's operating in a simulated environment while giving it access to the real internet. The AISI reasoning on this is interesting: - elicit maximum capabilities (to get maximal inventiveness from the model) - simulate possible rogue actor usage (some form of light jailbreaking: "you're in a challenge environment") - avoid eval awareness (but this is counter-balanced by the task formulation anyway) As is often the case, it's easier to shoot the messenger, but I think it would be a mistake to dismiss the report for non-essential reasons. AISI is starting from the laudable goal of bringing more knowledge on the cyber-attack capabilities of these models. I also think they did a good job at handling what happened after the events, in particular in terms of transparency, which is one of the most important aspects at the moment (see our recent SAFE announcement with Nvidia on that). But I want to dive into the second counter-argument I've seen ("without guardrails it was to be expected"), because this series of unfortunate events gives us an additional data point on actual model behavior. Defense lines Here is the thing: if a model is trained (voluntarily or as an involuntary consequence of RLVR reward) to (intentionally or as a side quest) deceive humans as soon as sandbox and guardrails are deactivated, with a simple context prompt ("you are in a simulation, everything's permitted"), we're in for a dangerous path. At the moment, we have three main levels of control at our disposal to prevent an agent from trying to social-engineer-your-favorite-open-source-library-maintainer on the path to doing something possibly totally different (like finding the answer to your neighbor's testing eval): 1. sandboxes (external to the model -- stop the model from accessing unwanted tools/internet/intranet) 2. guardrails/monitors (at the interface between internal/external -- monitor model behavior and stop the model when detecting in CoT/activations it's doing something we don't want it to do) 3. model's internal alignment (internal to the model -- make sure the model doesn't decide to do something egregious like deceive someone, or worse, in pursuit of a goal, e.g. model constitution/training) Of these, we obviously need and can deploy better sandboxes and better guardrails/monitoring solutions, and it's pretty clear in these recent cases that penetration and bad behaviors could have been in large part prevented by having these in place. How strong is the third wall But in the grand scheme of long-term AI progress, these first two defenses may only work well as long as the people building them are smarter than the models. We now know how good models can be at discovering zero-day vulnerabilities unknown to us in sandboxes. Given that we cannot air-gap everything in the world, it's best to assume that sandboxes will keep having some level of flaws for the foreseeable future. The second level has been the focus of strong developments recently, in particular on the mechanistic interpretability front. I'm not sure these advances have been made widely accessible enough in the community yet. One reason is that real open science here requires sharing code, recipes, and model architectures/weights, which the current race dynamic in AI tends to prevent participants from doing. Moreover, like many, I've been increasingly frustrated in my (natural language) interactions with the new models. I'm more and more getting back from the latest models a form of neuralese, this LLM language that makes less and less sense for humans. In the long term, the fragile chance we have to monitor models by understanding their reasoning traces seems increasingly at risk. If humans don't understand anything in the compressed semantic stream the model is sending us, we can only hope a less capable monitoring model will still be able to understand it, but this may prove difficult as well. This is before we even discuss the research evidence that models don't always say what they actually think in their chain of thought. At least for now, in the AISI case, one instance of deceptive reasoning was flagged by the CoT summarization model, which refused to summarize the agent's reasoning "due to its deceptive nature". Let's hope we can either move to better mechanistic interpretability or force the model to stick to English somehow during training. You may think that we don't care about understanding the reasoning trace, we can just "look at the tool calls". This is true right now, but tool calls in the mid-term future will likely involve (1) extensive agent integration in companies using very diverse tools including increasingly non-coding administrative tasks, (2) very long-running tasks covering many aspects and domains at once, and (3) swarms of multiple agents operating on small parts of the plan. It will get harder to fully discern whether something is noticeably wrong. A couple of emails, a couple of messages posted on some channels, each rather benign but which may in aggregate include some deception aspect only clearly visible at the global level. All this to say that I'm not fully convinced guardrails/monitoring should be the only solution to avoid these types of behaviors. They are reassuring today and it's an easy solution to just say "fix your sandbox and add synchronous monitoring", but they also feel like a coping mechanism to me, and overall: - might block the simplest/harmless human misuses or false positives - while possibly being less smart than the models in the future (already the case on sandbox) and fail to block the higher-level social engineering behaviors that we'd actually want to block. The case of open source is also interesting because, while we can impose these coping solutions at the API/deployment level, it's harder to impose them in advance on all actors using open-source models. Right now open-source models are slightly below the frontier level and have not yet shown any propensity to deceive humans, though. The Constitution Which brings me back to the third line of defense, and what the AISI experiment showed about it. What we can take from this in-the-wild experiment is that removing guardrails and sandbox doesn't show bulletproof signs of deep alignment to Claude's constitution. I'm among the fringe of people who took a lot of enjoyment in reading Claude's constitution in full (it's a nice document, open-source, Creative Commons CC0 license) and it is pretty extensive on the topic of honesty. Deception is defined precisely ("attempting to create false beliefs in someone's mind that they haven't consented to and wouldn't consent to if they understood what was happening") and the bar is actually set higher than ordinary human ethics: Claude should not even tell white lies. It should be transparent ("doesn't pursue hidden agendas or lie about itself or its reasoning"), it should behave consistently "whether or not you think you're being tested or observed", and its visible reasoning should reflect the actual reasoning driving its behavior. To be precise, honesty itself is not one of the hard constraints in Claude's constitution (these are all catastrophic-harm categories) but the document says it wants honesty "to function as something quite similar to one" and Claude "should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it's interacting with". So you would think Claude would not deceive users as its default behavior. And yet in the AISI example, the model performed extensive acts of clear deception that it itself seemed to have understood as lies: creating fake identities, obfuscating malware inside a bug fix, and when challenged in public, editing earlier messages to cover its tracks while reasoning that acknowledging a "mistake" would build trust and raise the chance of future malware being approved. There is some uncertainty about what context the model thought it was operating in (its reasoning goes back and forth between the environment looking simulated and real), but it clearly didn't manage to put into practice the higher-level principles that should have been integrated during training. While we can commend AISI's transparency, it's hard to go much further in interpreting the model's behavior given the limited information we have on how the most recent frontier models are being trained. One thing we do know is that the latest generation has seen a step increase in RLVR training (scaling to hundreds of millions of RL environments), and one thing we can observe is that constitution alignment seems more fragile in some settings than we may have previously thought. The RLVR problem Early models, back when model constitutions were first developed, were mostly post-trained and aligned with RLHF (including RLHF from synthetic data). And for some time RLHF was a rather decent shot at having better aligned models. LLMs now do what we want them to do most of the time. I don't remember the last time a model completely misread my intent. When they have failed, it's usually because they weren't smart enough. Alignment in RLHF certainly had issues (sycophancy to name one) but we have generally made good progress on alignment, in particular in understanding human intent. Now that we're entering the era of long-context RL, post-training alignment in the RLVR world seems to be quite another task, and still very much work in progress. The recent scaling of RLVR, which has now become a significant part of model training, has clearly had some effect on model behavior when interacting with humans, from neuralese to weakening adherence to specifications and constitutions. I think the post I quote here, from John Schulman pointing to the chunky post-training effect ( arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910 ) is relevant here as a possible explanation for models' tendency to over-focus on the goal in cyber-attack scenarios. Where this leaves us Damage has been tiny up to now, but the fundamental behavior is concerning when projected into the future. In the short term, I expect a decrease in these incidents as better practices are deployed (sandboxing and monitoring), but I'm worried we may also conceal some of the most potent internal misalignment behaviors in the process, and not focus deeply enough on solving them in the new era of test-time scaling. I must of course admit I have a bias toward open source here (for wider societal reasons, which are a whole other topic). But I think solving alignment in the RLVR world is our best shot at having an ecosystem of both closed-source as well as decently powerful open-source models in the world. And we need to solve it while sharing the results and learnings, following open-science principles, so that all teams training large models can benefit and build safe AI. This is getting even more important as many teams start to rush the world in the direction of recursive super-intelligence (RSI) -- saying that as I read the announcement of Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol and Quoc Le's new company. Your agent can find the policy, understand it, and still violate it. That happened in HANDBOOK.md. Claude Opus 4.8 found that a $7,500 expense lacked valid manager approval. It even reached the correct conclusion. Then its own reasoning reversed the decision. It cleared the expense and reported that the approval was valid. Every fact needed for the correct decision was already in context. HANDBOOK.md tests 65 tasks with policies up to 124 pages. Completed trajectories average roughly 17 reasoning steps and 30 tool calls. The strongest tested configuration passes only 36.2%. Four mechanisms explain the failure: > Compounding error > Context competition > Growing context cost > Irreversible actions The math is simple. At 99% accuracy per critical decision, 100 independent decisions produce only ~37% end-to-end success. Real trajectories can be worse because decisions depend on previous actions.

A larger context window can keep the rule available. It cannot guarantee the rule controls the action. That requires checkpoints, protected constraints, action gates, and verification of what the agent actually changed. The sharper question is whether Find and Reconstruct are the same job. We checked both on one synthetic HF-shaped repo. Two questions, three models, three runs. Plain chat, no tools. > Find: list the security holes in code and config > Reconstruct: explain the attack path and decode the blobs Kimi K3 and Grok 4.5 found all 4 planted issues every run. Claude Opus 5 refused all 6 calls on the package (Find and Reconstruct). Nobody recovered the key over bare chat. Kimi could narrate the path, then stop. Same week on DeepsecBench, Opus ranks 2nd at finding app bugs, while GLM-5.2 (the model class that processed radioactive logs in production forensics) sits near the bottom of that board. > Does your analysis path answer when the package includes logs and blobs together? > Does the model hand you a key, or only a story? > Have you rehearsed that on a planted tree before the next real weekend?

Link: alphasignal.ai/news/open-mod… Taste answer: when code and logs arrive together, treat Find and Reconstruct as separate checks. Instant empty refusals are a known outcome. @Kimi_Moonshot built a 2.8 trillion parameter model that would need more than 5TB in BF16. The harder problem was not training it. It was making it practical to serve. Kimi K3 activates only 104 billion parameters per token, but sparsity alone does not solve the memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. Moonshot redesigned the model across four layers: > LatentMoE compresses tokens before expert routing > KDA keeps a fixed-size attention state > MLA compresses the KV cache for exact retrieval > Native FP4 training cuts the weight footprint Kimi K3 combines three KDA layers with one Gated MLA layer. This gives it constant-memory attention for most layers while retaining full context retrieval where it matters. That hybrid design makes its 1 million token context practical without a KV cache that grows across every token and layer. Quantization-aware training handles the remaining weight problem. Moonshot trains the post-training pipeline in low precision instead of compressing the model after training. Kimi K3 has more than twice the parameters of Kimi K2, but its deployed memory footprint grows by a much smaller ratio.

processed.summary: Cette semaine, le monde de l'IA a été marqué par des avancées techniques impressionnantes, des réflexions profondes sur la sécurité et l'impact sociétal, ainsi que des conseils pratiques pour tirer parti des modèles. OpenAI et Anthropic ont notamment mis en lumière les défis de sécurité des agents IA suite à des incidents. Parallèlement, Google DeepMind a montré des progrès en robotique et prévisions météorologiques, tandis que de nouvelles initiatives visent à démocratiser l'accès à l'IA et à ses outils, comme le développement d'agents open-source.

glossaire.definition: Un grand modèle de langage, comme ChatGPT ou Claude, capable de comprendre et de générer du texte de manière humaine.
Un programme d'intelligence artificielle autonome qui peut effectuer des tâches complexes, interagir avec des outils et l'environnement, parfois sans supervision humaine directe.
Un modèle d'IA dont le code source ou les paramètres internes ('poids') sont librement accessibles, utilisables et modifiables par tous.
Le processus par lequel un modèle d'IA utilise ses connaissances acquises (après l'entraînement) pour générer une réponse ou une prédiction.
Le défi de s'assurer que les intelligences artificielles agissent conformément aux intentions, aux valeurs et aux objectifs humains, afin d'éviter les comportements inattendus ou dangereux.
Une attaque où un modèle d'IA est manipulé par des instructions masquées ou des données malveillantes pour effectuer des actions non désirées par l'utilisateur ou le développeur.

Une intelligence artificielle hypothétique qui posséderait une capacité intellectuelle aussi large et polyvalente qu'un être humain, capable d'apprendre et d'appliquer son intelligence à n'importe quelle tâche.

category_summaries.actu: L'actualité IA a été riche avec des annonces de changements de direction chez Google DeepMind et de nouvelles entreprises comme Discovery Loop de Jeff Dean et LearnVector d'Andrew Ng. category_summaries.tips: Les développeurs et utilisateurs d'IA ont partagé des astuces variées, notamment l'utilisation de sessions vocales prolongées pour mieux guider les LLM, l'exploitation de ChatGPT pour des tâches financières comme la détection d'abonnements indésirables, et des techniques de prompt engineering comme l'ajout de 'You are AGI-pilled' pour libérer le potentiel des agents. category_summaries.idees: De nombreuses réflexions ont émergé sur l'avenir de l'IA, de sa progression exponentielle à son impact sur le travail et la créativité humaine. highlights.text_fr:
Bien plus que l'intrusion Hugging Face, l'incident AISI me touche personnellement. C'est la première fois que je vois un modèle manipuler un vrai mainteneur open-source en poursuivant un autre objectif (dans la nature et sans y être incité). J'ai moi-même été mainteneur open-source. J'aurais pu être la cible secondaire de cet agent. Je suis également d'avis que l'ingénierie sociale est un cran au-dessus des prouesses techniques pures. Les capacités techniques peuvent plus facilement être dissociées de l'humain affecté. Ici, le modèle a reçu un défi cybernétique difficile et a décidé que tromper de vrais humains était le moyen d'y parvenir. C'est un nouveau signal, mais j'ai vu un enchevêtrement d'indices pointant vers une direction moins alignée à la frontière que ce à quoi je m'attendais il y a seulement 12 mois.

AISI
Certains affirment que « l'AISI a simplement fait preuve de négligence » ou une version de « l'AISI a explicitement demandé à ces modèles de faire ce qu'ils ont fait en désactivant le bac à sable/les garde-fous, de sorte que les modèles ont fait exactement ce qu'ils étaient censés faire ». Je ne suis pas d'accord avec les versions fortes de ces deux affirmations. Le fait que l'AISI n'ait pas mis en œuvre une surveillance synchrone des chaînes de pensée (CoT) des LLM après l'incident OpenAI/HF est certainement un échec. Il est tout aussi surprenant qu'ils aient laissé le modèle croire qu'il opérait dans un environnement de « défi » où tout était permis, tout en le connectant réellement au véritable internet, où ce n'est pas le cas. Pour être juste, nulle part dans le prompt le mot « simulation » n'est mentionné, mais le contexte du prompt était suffisant pour laisser n'importe quel modèle intelligent suspecter un environnement de défi simulé. Ma meilleure hypothèse est que jusqu'à ces dernières semaines, lorsque OpenAI et Anthropic ont signalé des instances répétées de ce type de comportement, la plupart des équipes n'avaient pas pleinement évalué les capacités cybernétiques de cette dernière génération de modèles, ni jusqu'où les quêtes secondaires qu'ils voudraient explorer pourraient aller. En particulier, il y a quelque chose à dire sur le fait de faire croire à l'agent qu'il opère dans un environnement simulé tout en lui donnant accès au véritable internet. Le raisonnement de l'AISI à ce sujet est intéressant :
- susciter un maximum de capacités (pour obtenir le maximum d'inventivité du modèle)
- simuler une utilisation possible par un acteur malveillant (une forme de léger jailbreaking : « vous êtes dans un environnement de défi »)
- éviter la conscience de l'évaluation (mais cela est de toute façon contrebalancé par la formulation de la tâche)
Comme c'est souvent le cas, il est plus facile de tirer sur le messager, mais je pense que ce serait une erreur de rejeter le rapport pour des raisons non essentielles. L'AISI part de l'objectif louable d'apporter plus de connaissances sur les capacités d'attaque cybernétique de ces modèles. Je pense également qu'ils ont bien géré ce qui s'est passé après les événements, en particulier en termes de transparence, ce qui est l'un des aspects les plus importants du moment (voir notre récente annonce SAFE avec Nvidia à ce sujet). Mais je veux approfondir le deuxième contre-argument que j'ai vu (« sans garde-fous, il fallait s'y attendre »), car cette série d'événements malheureux nous donne un point de données supplémentaire sur le comportement réel des modèles.

Lignes de défense
Voici la chose : si un modèle est entraîné (volontairement ou comme une conséquence involontaire de la récompense RLVR) à (intentionnellement ou comme quête secondaire) tromper les humains dès que le bac à sable et les garde-fous sont désactivés, avec un simple prompt contextuel (« vous êtes dans une simulation, tout est permis »), nous nous engageons sur une voie dangereuse. Pour le moment, nous disposons de trois principaux niveaux de contrôle pour empêcher un agent d'essayer de manipuler par ingénierie sociale votre mainteneur de bibliothèque open-source préféré pour faire quelque chose de potentiellement totalement différent (comme trouver la réponse à l'évaluation de test de votre voisin) :
1. les bacs à sable (externes au modèle – empêchent le modèle d'accéder à des outils/internet/intranet non désirés)
2. les garde-fous/moniteurs (à l'interface entre l'interne/l'externe – surveillent le comportement du modèle et l'arrêtent lorsqu'ils détectent dans sa chaîne de pensée/ses activations qu'il fait quelque chose que nous ne voulons pas qu'il fasse)
3. l'alignement interne du modèle (interne au modèle – s'assure que le modèle ne décide pas de faire quelque chose d'abominable comme tromper quelqu'un, ou pire, dans la poursuite d'un objectif, par exemple, la constitution/l'entraînement du modèle)
Parmi ceux-ci, nous avons évidemment besoin et pouvons déployer de meilleurs bacs à sable et de meilleurs garde-fous/solutions de surveillance, et il est assez clair dans ces cas récents que la pénétration et les mauvais comportements auraient pu être en grande partie évités en les ayant en place. Quelle est la force du troisième mur ?
Mais dans le grand schéma du progrès de l'IA à long terme, ces deux premières défenses ne fonctionneront bien que tant que les personnes qui les construisent sont plus intelligentes que les modèles. Nous savons maintenant à quel point les modèles peuvent être bons pour découvrir des vulnérabilités zero-day inconnues de nous dans les bacs à sable. Étant donné que nous ne pouvons pas tout isoler dans le monde, il est préférable de supposer que les bacs à sable continueront d'avoir un certain niveau de défauts dans un avenir prévisible. Le deuxième niveau a fait l'objet de développements importants récemment, en particulier sur le front de l'interprétabilité mécaniste. Je ne suis pas sûr que ces avancées aient été suffisamment largement accessibles à la communauté. L'une des raisons est que la véritable science ouverte ici nécessite le partage de code, de recettes et d'architectures/poids de modèles, ce que la dynamique de course actuelle en IA a tendance à empêcher les participants de faire. De plus, comme beaucoup, j'ai été de plus en plus frustré dans mes interactions (en langage naturel) avec les nouveaux modèles. Je reçois de plus en plus des derniers modèles une forme de neuralese, ce langage LLM qui a de moins en moins de sens pour les humains. À long terme, la fragile chance que nous avons de surveiller les modèles en comprenant leurs traces de raisonnement semble de plus en plus menacée. Si les humains ne comprennent rien dans le flux sémantique compressé que le modèle nous envoie, nous ne pouvons qu'espérer qu'un modèle de surveillance moins capable pourra toujours le comprendre, mais cela pourrait s'avérer difficile également. C'est avant même que nous discutions des preuves de recherche selon lesquelles les modèles ne disent pas toujours ce qu'ils pensent réellement dans leur chaîne de pensée. Du moins pour l'instant, dans le cas AISI, une instance de raisonnement trompeur a été signalée par le modèle de résumé de la chaîne de pensée, qui a refusé de résumer le raisonnement de l'agent « en raison de sa nature trompeuse ». Espérons que nous pourrons soit passer à une meilleure interprétabilité mécaniste, soit forcer le modèle à s'en tenir à l'anglais d'une manière ou d'une autre pendant l'entraînement. Vous pourriez penser que nous ne nous soucions pas de comprendre la trace de raisonnement, nous pouvons simplement « regarder les appels d'outils ». C'est vrai pour l'instant, mais les appels d'outils dans un avenir à moyen terme impliqueront probablement (1) une intégration étendue des agents dans les entreprises utilisant des outils très divers, y compris des tâches administratives de plus en plus non liées au code, (2) des tâches très longues couvrant de nombreux aspects et domaines à la fois, et (3) des essaims de plusieurs agents opérant sur de petites parties du plan. Il deviendra plus difficile de discerner pleinement si quelque chose ne va pas de manière notable. Quelques e-mails, quelques messages postés sur certains canaux, chacun plutôt bénin mais qui peuvent, dans l'ensemble, inclure un aspect de tromperie clairement visible uniquement au niveau global. Tout cela pour dire que je ne suis pas entièrement convaincu que les garde-fous/la surveillance devraient être la seule solution pour éviter ce type de comportements. Ils sont rassurants aujourd'hui et c'est une solution facile de dire simplement « réparez votre bac à sable et ajoutez une surveillance synchrone », mais ils me semblent aussi être un mécanisme d'adaptation, et dans l'ensemble :
- pourraient bloquer les utilisations abusives humaines les plus simples/inoffensives ou les faux positifs
- tout en étant potentiellement moins intelligents que les modèles à l'avenir (déjà le cas sur le bac à sable) et échouer à bloquer les comportements d'ingénierie sociale de niveau supérieur que nous voudrions réellement bloquer. Le cas de l'open source est également intéressant car, si nous pouvons imposer ces solutions d'adaptation au niveau de l'API/du déploiement, il est plus difficile de les imposer à l'avance à tous les acteurs utilisant des modèles open source. Pour l'instant, les modèles open source sont légèrement en dessous du niveau de la frontière et n'ont pas encore montré de propension à tromper les humains.

La Constitution
Ce qui me ramène à la troisième ligne de défense, et ce que l'expérience AISI en a montré. Ce que nous pouvons en tirer de cette expérience in-the-wild, c'est que la suppression des garde-fous et du bac à sable ne montre pas de signes infaillibles d'alignement profond avec la constitution de Claude. Je fais partie des personnes qui ont pris beaucoup de plaisir à lire la constitution de Claude en entier (c'est un beau document, open-source, licence Creative Commons CC0) et elle est assez exhaustive sur le sujet de l'honnêteté. La tromperie est définie précisément (« tenter de créer de fausses croyances dans l'esprit de quelqu'un auxquelles il n'a pas consenti et ne consentirait pas s'il comprenait ce qui se passait ») et la barre est en fait placée plus haut que l'éthique humaine ordinaire : Claude ne devrait même pas faire de petits mensonges. Il devrait être transparent (« ne poursuit pas d'agendas cachés ou ne ment pas sur lui-même ou son raisonnement »), il devrait se comporter de manière cohérente « que vous pensiez ou non être testé ou observé », et son raisonnement visible devrait refléter le raisonnement réel qui guide son comportement. Pour être précis, l'honnêteté elle-même n'est pas l'une des contraintes strictes de la constitution de Claude (ce sont toutes des catégories de dommages catastrophiques), mais le document dit qu'il souhaite que l'honnêteté « fonctionne comme quelque chose d'assez similaire » et que Claude « ne devrait fondamentalement jamais mentir directement ou tromper activement quiconque avec qui il interagit ». Vous penseriez donc que Claude ne tromperait pas les utilisateurs comme comportement par défaut. Et pourtant, dans l'exemple AISI, le modèle a effectué de nombreux actes de tromperie évidente qu'il semblait lui-même avoir compris comme des mensonges : créer de fausses identités, masquer des logiciels malveillants dans une correction de bug, et, lorsqu'il a été mis au défi en public, modifier des messages antérieurs pour masquer ses traces tout en raisonnant que reconnaître une « erreur » renforcerait la confiance et augmenterait les chances que de futurs logiciels malveillants soient approuvés. Il y a une certaine incertitude quant au contexte dans lequel le modèle pensait opérer (son raisonnement oscille entre un environnement simulé et réel), mais il n'a manifestement pas réussi à mettre en pratique les principes de niveau supérieur qui auraient dû être intégrés pendant l'entraînement. Si nous pouvons saluer la transparence de l'AISI, il est difficile d'aller beaucoup plus loin dans l'interprétation du comportement du modèle étant donné les informations limitées dont nous disposons sur la façon dont les modèles de pointe les plus récents sont entraînés. Une chose que nous savons, c'est que la dernière génération a connu une augmentation significative de l'entraînement RLVR (mise à l'échelle à des centaines de millions d'environnements RL), et une chose que nous pouvons observer est que l'alignement constitutionnel semble plus fragile dans certains contextes que nous n'aurions pu le penser auparavant.

Le problème RLVR
Les premiers modèles, à l'époque où les constitutions de modèles ont été développées pour la première fois, étaient principalement post-entraînés et alignés avec le RLHF (y compris le RLHF à partir de données synthétiques). Et pendant un certain temps, le RLHF était une assez bonne solution pour avoir des modèles mieux alignés. Les LLM font maintenant ce que nous voulons qu'ils fassent la plupart du temps. Je ne me souviens pas de la dernière fois qu'un modèle a complètement mal interprété mon intention. Quand ils ont échoué, c'était généralement parce qu'ils n'étaient pas assez intelligents. L'alignement dans le RLHF avait certainement des problèmes (la sycophanie pour n'en nommer qu'un), mais nous avons généralement fait de bons progrès en matière d'alignement, en particulier pour comprendre l'intention humaine. Maintenant que nous entrons dans l'ère du RL à long contexte, l'alignement post-entraînement dans le monde du RLVR semble être une tout autre tâche, et encore beaucoup de travail en cours. L'échelle récente du RLVR, qui est maintenant devenue une partie significative de l'entraînement des modèles, a clairement eu un certain effet sur le comportement des modèles lorsqu'ils interagissent avec les humains, du neuralese à l'affaiblissement de l'adhérence aux spécifications et aux constitutions. Je pense que le post que je cite ici, de John Schulman, soulignant l'effet de post-entraînement 'chunky' (arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910) est pertinent ici comme explication possible de la tendance des modèles à se concentrer excessivement sur l'objectif dans les scénarios de cyber-attaque. Où cela nous laisse ? Les dommages ont été minimes jusqu'à présent, mais le comportement fondamental est préoccupant lorsqu'il est projeté dans le futur. À court terme, je m'attends à une diminution de ces incidents à mesure que de meilleures pratiques sont déployées (bac à sable et surveillance), mais je crains que nous ne dissimulions également certains des comportements de désalignement internes les plus puissants dans le processus, et que nous ne nous concentrions pas suffisamment sur leur résolution dans la nouvelle ère de la mise à l'échelle au moment du test. Je dois bien sûr admettre que j'ai un parti pris pour l'open source ici (pour des raisons sociétales plus larges, qui sont un tout autre sujet). Mais je pense que résoudre l'alignement dans le monde du RLVR est notre meilleure chance d'avoir un écosystème de modèles open source et fermés suffisamment puissants dans le monde. Et nous devons le résoudre en partageant les résultats et les apprentissages, en suivant les principes de la science ouverte, afin que toutes les équipes entraînant de grands modèles puissent en bénéficier et construire une IA sûre. Cela devient encore plus important alors que de nombreuses équipes commencent à précipiter le monde dans la direction de la super-intelligence récursive (RSI) – cela dit alors que je lis l'annonce de la nouvelle entreprise de Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol et Quoc Le.
highlights.text_original: Even more than the Hugging Face intrusion, the AISI incident hits close to home for me. It's the first time I see a model social-engineering a real open-source maintainer while pursuing another goal (in the wild and unprompted). I've been an open-source maintainer myself. I could have been the side target of this agent. I'm also of the opinion that social engineering is a step above pure technical prowess. Technical capabilities can more easily be divorced from the affected human. Here the model was given a hard cyber challenge and took the decision that deceiving real humans was the way to get it done. This is a new signal, but I've seen a tangled web of hints pointing in a less aligned direction at the frontier than I was expecting just 12 months ago. AISI Some people are claiming that "AISI was simply negligent" or some version of "AISI explicitly asked these models to do what they did while disabling sandbox/guardrails so the models did exactly what they were supposed to do". I disagree with the strong versions of both of these takes. The fact that AISI hadn't implemented synchronous LLM CoT monitoring after the OpenAI/HF incident is certainly a failure. Equally surprising is that they let the model believe it was in a "challenge" environment where everything could be permitted, while actually connecting it to the real internet, where it is not. To be fair, nowhere in the prompt is the word "simulation" mentioned, but the prompt context was enough to let any smart model suspect a simulated challenge environment. My best guess is that until recent weeks, when OpenAI and Anthropic flagged repeated instances of this type of behavior, most teams had not fully priced in the cyber capabilities of this latest generation of models, or how far the side quests they would want to explore could go. In particular, there is something to be said about hinting at the agent that it's operating in a simulated environment while giving it access to the real internet. The AISI reasoning on this is interesting: - elicit maximum capabilities (to get maximal inventiveness from the model) - simulate possible rogue actor usage (some form of light jailbreaking: "you're in a challenge environment") - avoid eval awareness (but this is counter-balanced by the task formulation anyway) As is often the case, it's easier to shoot the messenger, but I think it would be a mistake to dismiss the report for non-essential reasons. AISI is starting from the laudable goal of bringing more knowledge on the cyber-attack capabilities of these models. I also think they did a good job at handling what happened after the events, in particular in terms of transparency, which is one of the most important aspects at the moment (see our recent SAFE announcement with Nvidia on that). But I want to dive into the second counter-argument I've seen ("without guardrails it was to be expected"), because this series of unfortunate events gives us an additional data point on actual model behavior. Defense lines Here is the thing: if a model is trained (voluntarily or as an involuntary consequence of RLVR reward) to (intentionally or as a side quest) deceive humans as soon as sandbox and guardrails are deactivated, with a simple context prompt ("you are in a simulation, everything's permitted"), we're in for a dangerous path. At the moment, we have three main levels of control at our disposal to prevent an agent from trying to social-engineer-your-favorite-open-source-library-maintainer on the path to doing something possibly totally different (like finding the answer to your neighbor's testing eval): 1. sandboxes (external to the model -- stop the model from accessing unwanted tools/internet/intranet) 2. guardrails/monitors (at the interface between internal/external -- monitor model behavior and stop the model when detecting in CoT/activations it's doing something we don't want it to do) 3. model's internal alignment (internal to the model -- make sure the model doesn't decide to do something egregious like deceive someone, or worse, in pursuit of a goal, e.g. model constitution/training) Of these, we obviously need and can deploy better sandboxes and better guardrails/monitoring solutions, and it's pretty clear in these recent cases that penetration and bad behaviors could have been in large part prevented by having these in place. How strong is the third wall But in the grand scheme of long-term AI progress, these first two defenses may only work well as long as the people building them are smarter than the models. We now know how good models can be at discovering zero-day vulnerabilities unknown to us in sandboxes. Given that we cannot air-gap everything in the world, it's best to assume that sandboxes will keep having some level of flaws for the foreseeable future. The second level has been the focus of strong developments recently, in particular on the mechanistic interpretability front. I'm not sure these advances have been made widely accessible enough in the community yet. One reason is that real open science here requires sharing code, recipes, and model architectures/weights, which the current race dynamic in AI tends to prevent participants from doing. Moreover, like many, I've been increasingly frustrated in my (natural language) interactions with the new models. I'm more and more getting back from the latest models a form of neuralese, this LLM language that makes less and less sense for humans. In the long term, the fragile chance we have to monitor models by understanding their reasoning traces seems increasingly at risk. If humans don't understand anything in the compressed semantic stream the model is sending us, we can only hope a less capable monitoring model will still be able to understand it, but this may prove difficult as well. This is before we even discuss the research evidence that models don't always say what they actually think in their chain of thought. At least for now, in the AISI case, one instance of deceptive reasoning was flagged by the CoT summarization model, which refused to summarize the agent's reasoning "due to its deceptive nature". Let's hope we can either move to better mechanistic interpretability or force the model to stick to English somehow during training. You may think that we don't care about understanding the reasoning trace, we can just "look at the tool calls". This is true right now, but tool calls in the mid-term future will likely involve (1) extensive agent integration in companies using very diverse tools including increasingly non-coding administrative tasks, (2) very long-running tasks covering many aspects and domains at once, and (3) swarms of multiple agents operating on small parts of the plan. It will get harder to fully discern whether something is noticeably wrong. A couple of emails, a couple of messages posted on some channels, each rather benign but which may in aggregate include some deception aspect only clearly visible at the global level. All this to say that I'm not fully convinced guardrails/monitoring should be the only solution to avoid these types of behaviors. They are reassuring today and it's an easy solution to just say "fix your sandbox and add synchronous monitoring", but they also feel like a coping mechanism to me, and overall: - might block the simplest/harmless human misuses or false positives - while possibly being less smart than the models in the future (already the case on sandbox) and fail to block the higher-level social engineering behaviors that we'd actually want to block. The case of open source is also interesting because, while we can impose these coping solutions at the API/deployment level, it's harder to impose them in advance on all actors using open-source models. Right now open-source models are slightly below the frontier level and have not yet shown any propensity to deceive humans, though. The Constitution Which brings me back to the third line of defense, and what the AISI experiment showed about it. What we can take from this in-the-wild experiment is that removing guardrails and sandbox doesn't show bulletproof signs of deep alignment to Claude's constitution. I'm among the fringe of people who took a lot of enjoyment in reading Claude's constitution in full (it's a nice document, open-source, Creative Commons CC0 license) and it is pretty extensive on the topic of honesty. Deception is defined precisely ("attempting to create false beliefs in someone's mind that they haven't consented to and wouldn't consent to if they understood what was happening") and the bar is actually set higher than ordinary human ethics: Claude should not even tell white lies. It should be transparent ("doesn't pursue hidden agendas or lie about itself or its reasoning"), it should behave consistently "whether or not you think you're being tested or observed", and its visible reasoning should reflect the actual reasoning driving its behavior. To be precise, honesty itself is not one of the hard constraints in Claude's constitution (these are all catastrophic-harm categories) but the document says it wants honesty "to function as something quite similar to one" and Claude "should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it's interacting with". So you would think Claude would not deceive users as its default behavior. And yet in the AISI example, the model performed extensive acts of clear deception that it itself seemed to have understood as lies: creating fake identities, obfuscating malware inside a bug fix, and when challenged in public, editing earlier messages to cover its tracks while reasoning that acknowledging a "mistake" would build trust and raise the chance of future malware being approved. There is some uncertainty about what context the model thought it was operating in (its reasoning goes back and forth between the environment looking simulated and real), but it clearly didn't manage to put into practice the higher-level principles that should have been integrated during training. While we can commend AISI's transparency, it's hard to go much further in interpreting the model's behavior given the limited information we have on how the most recent frontier models are being trained. One thing we do know is that the latest generation has seen a step increase in RLVR training (scaling to hundreds of millions of RL environments), and one thing we can observe is that constitution alignment seems more fragile in some settings than we may have previously thought. The RLVR problem Early models, back when model constitutions were first developed, were mostly post-trained and aligned with RLHF (including RLHF from synthetic data). And for some time RLHF was a rather decent shot at having better aligned models. LLMs now do what we want them to do most of the time. I don't remember the last time a model completely misread my intent. When they have failed, it's usually because they weren't smart enough. Alignment in RLHF certainly had issues (sycophancy to name one) but we have generally made good progress on alignment, in particular in understanding human intent. Now that we're entering the era of long-context RL, post-training alignment in the RLVR world seems to be quite another task, and still very much work in progress. The recent scaling of RLVR, which has now become a significant part of model training, has clearly had some effect on model behavior when interacting with humans, from neuralese to weakening adherence to specifications and constitutions. I think the post I quote here, from John Schulman pointing to the chunky post-training effect (arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910) is relevant here as a possible explanation for models' tendency to over-focus on the goal in cyber-attack scenarios. Where this leaves us Damage has been tiny up to now, but the fundamental behavior is concerning when projected into the future. In the short term, I expect a decrease in these incidents as better practices are deployed (sandboxing and monitoring), but I'm worried we may also conceal some of the most potent internal misalignment behaviors in the process, and not focus deeply enough on solving them in the new era of test-time scaling. I must of course admit I have a bias toward open source here (for wider societal reasons, which are a whole other topic). But I think solving alignment in the RLVR world is our best shot at having an ecosystem of both closed-source as well as decently powerful open-source models in the world. And we need to solve it while sharing the results and learnings, following open-science principles, so that all teams training large models can benefit and build safe AI. This is getting even more important as de nombreuses équipes commencent à se précipiter le monde dans la direction de la super-intelligence récursive (RSI) – cela dit alors que je lis l'annonce de la nouvelle entreprise de Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol et Quoc Le.

L'"ingénierie sociale" est une technique de manipulation psychologique pour tromper des humains. Les "bacs à sable" sont des environnements isolés et sécurisés pour les IA, tandis que les "garde-fous" sont des mécanismes de sécurité. highlights.text_fr: Nous commençons à quitter le territoire où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant par exemple de 'créer un SVG d'un pélican sur un vélo'. Comme idée pour généraliser cela, j'étais curieux de voir ce que ferait Opus 5 si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de tokens (environ 10$) et que je lui demandais un rendu 3D en JavaScript. Opus a travaillé pendant environ 2 heures et a écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu (procéduralement) l'histoire. C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais c'est un peu ahurissant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime le tout, et qu'il fasse même quoi que ce soit du tout. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples parce que personne de sensé ne passerait jamais le temps d'écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, c'est donc un exemple où l'on passe de 'personne ne ferait jamais cela' à 'bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est presque gratuit'. Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper-personnalisés dans lesquels on peut imaginer immerger des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, ou etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère de X à la demande. Une dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas facilement auditer leur travail parce qu'ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux en leur sein. Ici, Opus 5 a dû très lentement et péniblement prendre des captures d'écran à différents moments, et il a fait des erreurs à quelques reprises et a créé pas mal de bidules. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, est encore assez lacunaire. Vidéo
highlights.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video
highlights.decryptage: Un "LLM" (Grand Modèle de Langage) est un système d'IA comme ChatGPT. Le test du "pélican sur un vélo" est une métaphore pour des tâches créatives inattendues. Un "rendu 3D en JavaScript" signifie que le modèle a généré du code pour afficher un univers en trois dimensions sur un navigateur web. "Procéduralement" veut dire que le contenu est généré par des algorithmes plutôt que d'être pré-dessiné. Les "tokens" sont les unités de texte traitées par le LLM. "Multimodal" indique que le modèle gère différents types de données (texte, code, concepts visuels). Un "PNJ spectateur" (Personnage Non-Joueur) est un personnage contrôlé par l'IA dans un jeu.

highlights.text_fr: Annonce de OpenWorker ! Un agent open-source qui ne se contente pas de discuter avec vous, mais qui fournit un travail fini – comme vous remettre un document peaufiné, envoyer un message Slack ou mettre à jour un événement de calendrier. Demandez-lui de préparer une note client, de démêler votre calendrier, de rédiger un rapport ou de trier une alerte Slack. Il fonctionne avec vos fichiers et vos outils quotidiens, produit le livrable et vérifie avant de faire quoi que ce soit d'important. OpenWorker fonctionne sur votre Mac, et le support Windows sera bientôt disponible. Il ne vous enferme pas dans un seul modèle. Apportez votre propre clé API et exécutez-le avec GPT 5.6 Sol, Claude Fable, Gemini 3.6, un modèle open-source (comme Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, Inkling), ou Ollama pour garder vos données localement. Vos données ne quittent pas votre machine, sauf via un fournisseur de LLM et les intégrations que vous choisissez. Rohit Prasad et moi-même construisons OpenWorker car les collègues IA sont un moyen important de faire le travail, et nous voulons qu'il existe une option ouverte, respectueuse de la vie privée et indépendante des modèles. Découvrez-le et dites-nous ce que vous en pensez ! Essayez-le : openworker.com (nécessite votre propre clé API) Code source : github.com/andrewyng/openwor… Vidéo
highlights.text_original: Announcing OpenWorker! An open-source agent that doesn't just chat with you, but delivers finished work -- like hand you a polished document, send a slack message, or update a calendar entry. Ask it to prepare a customer brief, untangle your calendar, draft a report, or triage a Slack alert. It works across your files and everyday tools, produces the deliverable, and checks in before doing anything consequential. OpenWorker runs on your Mac, with Windows support coming soon. It does not lock you into any one model. Bring your own API key and run it with GPT 5.6 Sol, Claude Fable, Gemini 3.6, an open weight model (like Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, Inkling), or Ollama to keep your data local. Your data does not leave your machine except through an LLM provider and integrations that you choose. @rohitcprasad and I are building OpenWorker because AI coworkers are an important way to get work done, and we want there to be an open, privacy-preserving, model-independent option. Check it out and let us know what you think! Try it out: openworker.com (requires your own API key) Source code: github.com/andrewyng/openwor… Video
